subject: chemistry
title: Tests for ions
key_idea: Anions and ammonium ions are identified by simple test-tube reactions. Carbonate gives CO₂ with acid, sulfate gives a white precipitate with barium ions, halides give coloured precipitates with silver ions, and ammonium gives ammonia with warm alkali. The tests are done in the order carbonate, sulfate, halide.

blocks.text: Each anion has a test that gives a clear result. This section covers carbonate, sulfate and halide ions.

rows: Fizzing. The gas turns limewater milky
Fizzing. The gas turns limewater milky
White precipitate, soluble in dilute ammonia
Cream precipitate, soluble in concentrated ammonia
Pale yellow precipitate, insoluble in ammonia

items: The barium chloride is acidified with hydrochloric acid to remove carbonate ions, which would give a white precipitate of BaCO₃.
The silver nitrate is acidified with nitric acid to remove carbonate ions, which would give a precipitate of Ag₂CO₃.
Ammonia is then used to tell the three halides apart.
Carbonate gives CO₂ with acid. Sulfate gives a white precipitate with barium ions.
Halides give coloured precipitates with silver ions, and ammonia tells them apart.

blocks.text: When you test an unknown compound for anions, the order matters. The order is carbonate, then sulfate, then halide.

items: Carbonate is tested first because it would give a precipitate in the sulfate and halide tests: BaCO₃ and Ag₂CO₃ are both insoluble.
Sulfate is tested before halide because silver sulfate is only sparingly soluble. Sulfate could give a precipitate with silver ions.
After the carbonate and sulfate are removed, a precipitate with silver nitrate must be due to a halide.

diagram.alt: A sequencing activity. Put the tests for the anions in the correct order.
steps: Add dilute acid. Fizzing shows carbonate
Add acidified barium chloride. A white precipitate shows sulfate
Add acidified silver nitrate. A coloured precipitate shows a halide
Add ammonia. Dissolving tells you which halide

items: Test for carbonate, then sulfate, then halide.
The earlier tests remove ions that would interfere with the later ones.

blocks.text: Ammonium ions are the cation tested here. This section covers the test and the equation.

items.text: Add sodium hydroxide solution to the sample.
Warm the mixture gently. Ammonia gas is given off.
Hold damp red litmus paper at the mouth of the tube. It turns blue.

blocks.text: Ammonia has a sharp smell. Hydrogen chloride from concentrated hydrochloric acid gives white smoke with it.

diagram.alt: A predictor. Pick an ion to see the test, the result and the ionic equation.

options.label: Ammonium
results: Ammonia gas turns damp red litmus blue

items: Ammonium ions give ammonia when warmed with alkali.
Ammonia turns damp red litmus paper blue.

checks.q: Describe the test for sulfate ions and write the ionic equation.
checks.a: Add dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution. A white precipitate forms. Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s)

checks.q: A solid gives bubbles with dilute acid, then a cream precipitate with acidified silver nitrate. Name the two anions.
checks.a: Carbonate, from the bubbles of CO₂. Bromide, from the cream precipitate.

checks.q: Explain why the test for carbonate is done before the test for halide ions.
checks.a: Carbonate ions give a precipitate of Ag₂CO₃ with silver nitrate, which could be mistaken for a halide. The acid removes the carbonate ions first.

blocks.text: This part covers the test-tube tests for some transition metal ions. Each gives a hydroxide precipitate with sodium hydroxide.

rows: Dissolves to a deep blue solution
Green precipitate, going brown in air
Pale brown precipitate, darkening in air
Dissolves to a dark green solution

items: The precipitates are the metal hydroxides, for example Cu²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Cu(OH)₂.
Cr(OH)₃ is amphoteric, so it dissolves in excess alkali.
Iron(II) and manganese(II) hydroxides are oxidised by air, so they darken on standing.

blocks.text: This part covers simple test-tube reactions of some metal ions in aqueous solution.

rows: Pale blue precipitate, insoluble in excess
Orange-brown precipitate and bubbles of CO₂
White precipitate and bubbles of CO₂

items: M³⁺ ions are more acidic than M²⁺ ions. Their carbonates are not formed, and CO₂ is given off instead.
The higher charge on M³⁺ makes the charge/size ratio larger, so it polarises the water ligands more and releases H⁺ more easily.
Al(OH)₃ is amphoteric: it dissolves in both acid and excess sodium hydroxide.
